_about: Machine-readable form of red_flags.md. Thresholds and citations are copied from that file (retrieved 2026-11-20). Do not change a number here without changing red_flags.md and its source.

rules.title: High temperature in a baby under 3 months
rules.body: A temperature of {value} was logged at {time}. For a baby under 3 months, a temperature of 38°C or higher needs urgent medical help. Contact a doctor now or go to the nearest hospital emergency department.

rules.title: High temperature in a baby 3 to 6 months old
rules.body: A temperature of {value} was logged at {time}. The NHS says a baby 3 to 6 months old with a temperature of 39°C or higher needs urgent medical help. Contact a doctor now or call your local emergency number.

citations.title: High temperature (fever) in children

rules.title: High temperature for more than 5 days
rules.body: Temperatures of 38°C or higher have been logged since {since}. The NHS says to get medical advice when a high temperature lasts 5 days or more. Contact a doctor.

citations.title: When to get urgent medical help for babies and children under 5
High temperature (fever) in children

rules.title: Fever for more than 24 hours
rules.body: Temperatures of 38°C or higher have been logged since {since}. HealthyChildren.org (AAP) says to call the doctor when a child younger than 2 years has a fever for more than 24 hours.

citations.title: Fever: When to Call the Pediatrician

rules.title: Temperature above 40°C more than once
rules.body: Temperatures above 40°C were logged {count} times since {since}. HealthyChildren.org (AAP) says to call the doctor when the temperature rises above 40°C repeatedly, at any age.

citations.title: Fever: When to Call the Pediatrician

rules.title: Low temperature
rules.body: A temperature of {value} was logged at {time}. The NHS says a temperature lower than 36°C needs urgent medical help. Check it 2 more times within 10 minutes. If it stays low, call your local emergency number or go to the emergency department.

citations.title: When to get urgent medical help for babies and children under 5

rules.title: No wet {nappy} for 12 hours
rules.body: The last wet {nappy} was logged at {time}, {hours} hours ago. The NHS says no wet {nappies} for at least 12 hours is a sign of serious illness. Get medical help now. If you changed a wet {nappy} and did not log it, you can ignore this.

citations.title: When to get urgent medical help for babies and children under 5

rules.title: No wet {nappy} for 8 hours
rules.body: The last wet {nappy} was logged at {time}, {hours} hours ago. The NHS lists no wet {nappy} in the past 8 hours (in a baby who cries all the time) as a reason to call for help, and Pregnancy, Birth and Baby says to see a doctor if a baby has had no wet {nappy} for 4 to 6 hours with other signs of dehydration. If you are worried, contact a doctor. If you changed a wet {nappy} and did not log it, you can ignore this.

citations.title: Soothing a crying baby
Dehydration in babies

rules.title: Black poo
rules.body: A black poo was logged at {time}. After the first meconium poos, black poo can be a sign of blood. Talk to your doctor about it soon.

citations.title: The Many Colors of Baby Poop

rules.title: Red poo or blood in poo
rules.body: A red poo was logged at {time}. Any amount of blood in poo should be checked by a doctor. Contact a doctor soon (the NHS says to ask for an urgent GP appointment).

citations.title: The Many Colors of Baby Poop
Reflux in babies

rules.title: Pale or grey poo
rules.body: A pale or grey poo was logged at {time}. Pale poo can be a sign of a liver problem or jaundice. Tell a doctor or health visitor as soon as possible.

citations.title: The Many Colors of Baby Poop
How to change your baby's nappy

rules.title: Allergic reaction after food
rules.body: An allergic reaction was logged at {time} ({foods}). Breathing problems, a swollen throat or tongue, or a child who goes pale and floppy is a medical emergency: call your local emergency number now. For milder signs, such as a rash or swollen lips, talk to a doctor before you give this food again.

citations.title: Food allergies in babies and young children
Allergic and anaphylactic reactions

wet_nappy_baseline.text: The NHS says a baby should have around 6 wet {nappies} a day from a few days after the birth.
